title: The 50-30-20 budgeting rule
transcript: Welcome back to Money in Minutes. Today I want to talk about a simple budgeting method called the fifty-thirty-twenty rule. Here's how it works. You take your monthly income after tax and split it into three parts. Fifty percent goes to needs, like rent, groceries and transport. Thirty percent goes to wants, things like eating out, streaming services or that new pair of shoes. And the last twenty percent goes to savings or paying off debt. Now, I know what you're thinking: in a big city, rent alone can be more than half your salary. That's true, and the rule isn't perfect. But it gives you a starting point. If your needs take sixty percent, try cutting your wants to twenty. The important thing is to save something every month, even if it's a small amount. Small habits really do add up over time.

title: Is remote work here to stay?
transcript: So, the big question everyone keeps asking me is: is remote work here to stay? And my honest answer is, it depends on what you mean by remote. Fully remote companies are actually a minority. What we're seeing in most places is a hybrid model, where people come into the office two or three days a week. Interestingly, the research suggests that productivity isn't really the issue. Most people get just as much done at home. The real challenge is something harder to measure: the informal learning that happens when junior employees sit next to experienced colleagues. You overhear how someone handles a difficult client call, you ask a quick question, and you pick things up without even noticing. That's very hard to replicate on video calls. So if I were running a company, I wouldn't ask whether people should come back. I'd ask which days, and for what kind of work, being together actually adds value.

title: Lecture: the urban heat island
transcript: Today we're going to look at a phenomenon called the urban heat island effect. Simply put, cities tend to be warmer than the surrounding countryside, sometimes by as much as five to seven degrees Celsius at night. Why does this happen? Well, there are three main factors. First, materials like asphalt and concrete absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset. Second, cities have fewer trees and less vegetation, which normally cool the air through a process called evapotranspiration. And third, human activity itself, cars, air conditioners and factories, generates a lot of heat. Now, this isn't just a matter of comfort. Higher temperatures increase energy demand, worsen air quality and, during heat waves, can be dangerous for elderly people. Some cities are responding with green roofs, more parks and lighter-colored pavements that reflect sunlight. We'll look at a case study from Singapore in a moment.

title: Lecture: the rent control debate
transcript: Let's turn now to one of the most contentious policies in urban economics: rent control. The intuition behind it is straightforward. If rents are rising faster than incomes, capping them should protect existing tenants from displacement. And in the short run, the evidence suggests it does exactly that. Tenants in controlled units tend to stay put longer and are less likely to be forced out of their neighborhoods. The problem is what happens over a longer horizon. A well-known study of San Francisco found that landlords subject to new controls were significantly more likely to convert their buildings into condominiums or redevelop them, which reduced the supply of rental housing by around fifteen percent. In other words, the policy protected the people who already had apartments, but arguably pushed up rents for everyone else. Now, I'm not suggesting this settles the debate. Proponents point out that newer versions, so-called rent stabilization, allow moderate annual increases and exempt new construction, precisely to avoid discouraging investment. So the real question isn't whether rent control is good or bad in the abstract. It's how a specific design balances the interests of current tenants against those of future ones. Keep that framing in mind for this week's reading.

title: Podcast: are we really goldfish?
transcript: I want to push back a little on the way we usually talk about screen time. The standard narrative goes something like this: our phones are designed to be addictive, our attention spans are shrinking, and we're all doomed to become goldfish. And look, there's some truth in that. Many apps are explicitly engineered to maximize engagement, often with features like infinite scroll and autoplay that remove any natural stopping point. But the claim that our attention spans have collapsed is shakier than it sounds. That famous statistic comparing us to goldfish? Nobody has ever been able to trace it back to an actual study. What the research does suggest is that we've become much more selective. We'll happily binge a ten-hour documentary series, yet abandon an article after two paragraphs if it doesn't grab us. So perhaps the problem isn't that we can't pay attention, but that we're constantly being asked to decide what deserves it. And that kind of decision fatigue is exhausting in its own right.

title: Lecture: how memory rewrites itself
transcript: For a long time, memory was thought of as a kind of storage system. You experience something, it gets recorded, and later you retrieve it, more or less intact. The research of the last few decades has pretty much dismantled that picture. What we now understand is that every time you recall a memory, you're actually reconstructing it, and in the process it becomes temporarily unstable. This is known as reconsolidation. In practical terms, it means that memories can be altered each time they're retrieved, by new information, by the way a question is phrased, even by your current mood. Elizabeth Loftus's classic experiments illustrate this nicely. Participants who watched a video of a car accident gave higher speed estimates when asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed into each other, compared with those asked about cars that hit each other. Some even remembered broken glass that wasn't there. The implications for eyewitness testimony are obvious, and frankly rather troubling. For your assignment, I'd like you to consider what this means for how police interviews should be conducted.
